Q: What was Jamaica like when you were growing up?

A: Beautiful. That's the word. I know people say that but it's true — the colours, the heat, the smell of everything. Mango trees in the yard. My grandmother kept chickens. It was poor, mind you, we didn't have much, but it was alive in a way England took some getting used to. England was very quiet compared to home. Very grey and quiet.

Q: Why did you come to England?

A: My aunt had come the year before and she wrote back saying there was work, the pay was good, come and see. I was seventeen and I thought why not. My mother was not happy about it — she cried at the dock. I thought she was being dramatic. [shakes head] When my own daughter went to university in Leeds I stood in the kitchen and cried for an hour. So I understand her better now.

Q: What was the hardest part of arriving?

A: The signs. "No Coloureds, No Irish, No Dogs." I'd been told about them but seeing them was different. You'd go to a house for a room and the woman would open the door and close it again before you'd said a word. I was a churchgoing girl from a respectable family and they looked at me like I was nothing. That takes something from you. You build it back, but it takes something.

Q: How did you keep going through that?

A: The church. Always the church. And the community — there were a lot of us in the same situation and you looked out for each other. And I'm stubborn. [laughs] My mother always said I was too stubborn and for once in my life that was the right thing to be. I wasn't going to let them win. I had as much right to be there as anyone. More, some would say, given what Jamaica contributed to the war.

Q: What do you want your grandchildren to know about your life?

A: That it wasn't easy and I did it anyway. That's what I want them to know. They have so much more than I had — so many doors open that were closed to me — and sometimes I think they don't know it. I don't say that to make them feel bad. I say it so they know the doors didn't open by themselves. People pushed them open. I want them to know somebody pushed.
